q: What is the difference between a model's parameters and its hyperparameters?
o: Parameters are set by hand before training; hyperparameters are learned from the data
There is no difference; the two words mean the same
Parameters belong to regression models and hyperparameters to classification models
Parameters are learned from the training data; hyperparameters are chosen before training starts
e:
Parameters are the numbers the model learns while training, such as the weights of a linear model or the split values of a tree.
Hyperparameters are settings you choose before training, such as the learning rate, the maximum depth of a tree or the strength of regularization.
You find good hyperparameters by trying values and measuring on validation data, not by training them.
r: Parameters are learned; hyperparameters are chosen.

q: Why do you keep a test set that the model never sees during training?
o: To make training run faster on a smaller dataset
To estimate how the model will perform on new, unseen data
To choose the best hyperparameters
To balance the classes before training
e:
A model can memorize its training data, so its score on that data says little about the future.
The test set stands in for new data: you measure it once, at the end, to get an honest estimate.
If you tune hyperparameters on it, it stops being honest. Use a separate validation set (or cross-validation) for tuning.
r: Test data gives an honest estimate; do not tune on it.

q: Which of these tasks is a regression problem?
o: Deciding whether a card payment is fraud
Assigning a photo to one of ten product categories
Predicting how many minutes a delivery will take
Predicting whether a customer will cancel next month
e:
Regression predicts a number on a continuous scale, like minutes, price or temperature.
The other three predict a category (fraud or not, which category, cancel or not), so they are classification.
The names can confuse: logistic regression is a classification method, because it predicts a class (through a probability).
r: Regression predicts a number, classification predicts a category.

q: You have purchase histories for 50,000 customers but no labels, and you want to find groups of similar customers. What kind of learning is this?
o: Unsupervised learning (clustering)
Supervised regression
Supervised classification
Reinforcement learning
e:
Supervised learning needs labels (the right answers) to learn from. Here there are none, so you look for structure in the data itself.
Grouping similar items is clustering, the most common unsupervised task (k-means is a classic example).
Reinforcement learning is different: an agent learns by acting and receiving rewards.
r: No labels, find structure: unsupervised.

q: A model scores 99% on its training data and 70% on new data. What is this called?
o: Underfitting
Data drift
Overfitting
Class imbalance
e:
The model has memorized details and noise of the training set instead of learning the general pattern, so it does not carry over to new data.
Underfitting is the opposite: the score is poor on both training and new data.
Typical fixes: more data, a simpler model, regularization, or fewer features.
r: Great on training, poor on new data: overfitting.

q: A table lists houses with the columns size, rooms, neighbourhood and price. You want to predict the price. Which one is the label?
o: Size, because it is the most important column
Neighbourhood, because it is text
The whole table
Price, the value you want to predict
e:
The label (or target) is the value the model must predict. The other columns are features: the inputs it uses to do so.
Features can be numbers or categories. A text column such as neighbourhood is not a label, it just needs encoding first.
Which column is the label depends on the question you ask, not on the type of the column.
r: Label = what you predict; features = what you predict from.

q: Both the training error and the validation error are high and close to each other. What does that suggest?
o: High variance: the model is overfitting
High bias: the model is too simple for the pattern (underfitting)
Data leakage from the validation set
A validation set that is too small
e:
When a model is bad even on the data it trained on, it cannot capture the pattern: that is high bias, or underfitting.
Overfitting (high variance) looks different: low training error but much higher validation error.
Fixes for high bias: a more flexible model, better features, less regularization. More data alone will not help much.
r: Both errors high: bias. A big gap between them: variance.

q: Only 0.5% of card payments are fraud. A model that always predicts "not fraud" has what accuracy?
e:
Accuracy is the share of correct predictions. If 995 of every 1,000 payments are legitimate, always saying "not fraud" is right 99.5% of the time.
Yet this model catches no fraud at all. With imbalanced classes, accuracy hides the failure.
Look at precision, recall or PR-AUC for the rare class instead.
r: Accuracy misleads when one class is rare.

q: A screening model looks for a serious disease, and missing a sick patient is much worse than a false alarm. Which metric matters most?
o: Precision
Recall (sensitivity)
Accuracy
Specificity
e:
Recall is the share of real positives the model finds: TP / (TP + FN). It drops when sick patients are missed.
Precision says how many alarms were right, which matters when false alarms are expensive. Specificity measures how well healthy people are cleared, the opposite concern.
In practice you pick a threshold that reaches the recall you need and then check what precision you pay for it.
r: Missing positives is costly: maximise recall.

q: A spam filter flags 100 emails and 80 of them really are spam. The inbox held 200 spam emails in total. What are precision and recall?
o: Precision 0.4, recall 0.4
Precision 0.4, recall 0.8
Precision 0.8, recall 0.8
Precision 0.8, recall 0.4
e:
Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 80 / 100 = 0.8: of what you flagged, how much was right.
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 80 / 200 = 0.4: of all the real spam, how much you caught.
Precision uses the flagged emails as its denominator; recall uses the real positives.
r: Precision: out of flagged. Recall: out of real.

q: You standardize every feature using the mean and standard deviation of the whole dataset, and only then split it into train and test. What is wrong?
o: Test-set statistics leaked into the preprocessing, so the test score can look better than reality
Scaling before splitting makes the model overfit
Nothing: scaling does not learn anything from the labels
Standardization must always be done after training
e:
Scaling learns something from the data: the mean and the standard deviation. If those include the test rows, information from the test set reached the training process. This is data leakage.
The fix is to fit the scaler on the training data only and then apply it to the test data. A scikit-learn `Pipeline` does this for you, also inside cross-validation.
Labels are not needed for leakage: any statistic that peeks at the test set counts.
r: Fit preprocessing on training data only.

q: Which regularization penalty can push some coefficients of a linear model to exactly zero?
o: L2 (ridge)
Both do it equally
L1 (lasso)
Neither: regularization only makes coefficients smaller, never zero
e:
L1 adds the sum of absolute coefficient values to the loss. Its shape pushes weak features to exactly zero, so it also works as a form of feature selection.
L2 adds the sum of squares. It shrinks all coefficients toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero.
Elastic net mixes the two.
r: L1 gives sparse models; L2 shrinks smoothly.

q: What does 5-fold cross-validation do?
o: Trains one model on 80% of the data and tests it on the other 20%, repeated five times with the same split
Draws five random samples with replacement and averages the models
Trains five models with different random seeds on all the data and averages them
Splits the data into five parts and trains five models, each time validating on a different part, then averages the scores
e:
Each fold is used exactly once as validation data while the other four train the model. The five scores are averaged, and their spread tells you how stable the result is.
It uses all the data for both training and validation, which helps when the dataset is small.
It costs k training runs.
r: k folds, k models, each fold validates once.

q: You tried 50 hyperparameter combinations and reported the best score on the test set. What is the problem?
o: The score is optimistic: the test set guided the choice, so it is no longer unseen
50 combinations is too few to be reliable
The score is pessimistic, since the best model was picked
None: this is how the test set is meant to be used
e:
Choosing the best of 50 results on the same data selects partly on luck. The winning score is biased upward, and the test set no longer measures performance on unseen data.
Tune on a validation set or with cross-validation. Touch the test set once, for the final model.
If you must tune a lot and still want an honest number, use nested cross-validation.
r: Select on validation data, report on test data.

q: Why does a single, very deep decision tree tend to overfit?
o: It cannot split on numeric features
It can keep splitting until it fits even the noise of the training set, so small changes in the data change the tree a lot
Trees need scaled features, and unscaled data confuses them
Trees are always too shallow to learn real patterns
e:
Without limits (maximum depth, minimum samples per leaf, pruning), a tree keeps splitting until each leaf is nearly pure, even if it only memorizes noise.
That gives low bias and high variance: a slightly different training set produces a very different tree.
Limiting the depth or averaging many trees (a forest) reduces the variance.
r: Deep trees memorize: low bias, high variance.

q: What helps a random forest generalize better than one deep decision tree?
o: It builds trees one after another, each fixing the mistakes of the previous one
It prunes the tree with gradient descent
It trains many trees on bootstrap samples with random subsets of features and averages their votes, which lowers variance
It uses more training data than a single tree
e:
The trees in a random forest are trained independently, each on a bootstrap sample of the rows and with a random subset of features at each split. Their errors are less correlated, and averaging cancels much of the noise.
Building trees one after another describes boosting, not a random forest: there the trees are built in sequence and each one learns from the errors of the ensemble so far.
A forest keeps the low bias of deep trees but reduces their variance.
r: Forest = bagging + random features: lower variance.

q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off and how you react to each symptom.
a:
- Bias: error from a model too simple for the pattern. Symptom: high error on training and validation data (underfitting).
- Variance: error from a model too sensitive to the training sample. Symptom: low training error and much higher validation error (overfitting).
- More model capacity lowers bias and raises variance; the best model sits in between.
- High bias: richer features, a more flexible model, less regularization.
- High variance: more data, a simpler model, stronger regularization, fewer features, bagging or early stopping.
- Plot learning curves (error against training size) to see which case you are in.

q: Only 1% of your examples are positive. What is a sensible way to start?
o: Oversample the positives in the whole dataset and then split it into train and test
Report accuracy: it is the standard metric for classifiers
Use a stratified split and judge the model with precision, recall or PR-AUC instead of accuracy
Use a bigger model: imbalance disappears with enough capacity
e:
A stratified split keeps the 1% share in every part, so each one has positives to learn from and to be tested on. Accuracy would reward always predicting the majority class, so use metrics for the rare class.
Resampling is fine, but only on the training part: oversampling before the split puts copies of the same row in train and test (leakage).
Class weights or threshold tuning often work as well as resampling.
r: Stratify, pick the right metric, resample only training data.

q: Positives are very rare (0.1%). Why can ROC-AUC look excellent while the model is poor at finding them?
o: ROC-AUC ignores the positive class
The false positive rate divides by the huge number of negatives, so many false alarms barely move it, while precision collapses
ROC-AUC is computed from accuracy
ROC-AUC cannot be calculated with imbalanced classes
e:
The ROC curve plots recall against the false positive rate, FP / (FP + TN). When negatives dominate, TN is enormous, so even thousands of false alarms leave the rate tiny.
Precision, TP / (TP + FP), is hit directly by those false alarms. A PR curve or average precision shows the problem that ROC hides.
ROC-AUC is still defined with imbalance; it just answers a different question from the one you usually care about.
r: Rare positives: check the PR curve, not only ROC.

q: A binary classifier has a ROC-AUC of 0.5. What does that mean?
o: Its accuracy is always exactly 50%
Half of its predictions are wrong
Its probabilities are perfectly calibrated
It ranks examples no better than chance: a random positive scores above a random negative half of the time
e:
ROC-AUC is the probability that the model gives a higher score to a random positive than to a random negative. 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is a perfect ranking, and below 0.5 the ranking is inverted.
Accuracy depends on the threshold and the class balance, so an AUC of 0.5 does not fix it at 50%.
AUC says nothing about calibration.
r: AUC 0.5 = random ranking.

q: A model outputs the probability of fraud. You raise the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.8. What usually happens?
o: Precision goes up and recall goes down
Precision goes down and recall goes up
Both precision and recall go up
Nothing changes, because ROC-AUC does not depend on the threshold
e:
A higher threshold means the model flags fewer cases, and only those it is most sure about. Usually that gives fewer false positives (higher precision) and more missed positives (lower recall). F1 moves depending on which effect is bigger.
ROC-AUC does not depend on the threshold, but precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrix do.
Choose the threshold from the cost of each error, not by default at 0.5.
r: Higher threshold: precision up, recall down.

q: A churn model has an offline AUC of 0.99 but only about 0.6 in production. One of its features is `days_since_account_closed`. What is the most likely cause?
o: Target leakage: the feature is only known after the customer has already left
Class imbalance in the training data
Too many trees in the ensemble
Underfitting: the model is too simple
e:
A feature that is only filled in after the outcome carries the answer. In training it makes the task almost trivial; at prediction time it is missing or empty, so the score collapses.
Ask of every feature: will I know this value at the moment I need the prediction?
A suspiciously high offline score is a typical sign of leakage.
r: Too good to be true: look for target leakage.

q: You must forecast next week's demand using three years of weekly data. Which validation scheme fits?
o: Shuffled 5-fold cross-validation
A random 80/20 split
Time-ordered splits: train on earlier weeks and validate on later ones (for example `TimeSeriesSplit`)
Leave-one-out cross-validation
e:
In production the model only sees the past and predicts the future. Validation must copy that. Shuffling lets the model train on weeks after the ones it is tested on, which leaks information about trends and seasonality, and the scores come out too good.
`TimeSeriesSplit` makes folds where the training window always comes before the validation window.
Keep a final period at the end as the untouched test set.
r: Time data: validate forward in time.

q: Each patient has many images in the dataset. Random k-fold gives 0.97 accuracy, but at a new hospital the model scores 0.80. What should you change?
o: Add more trees
Increase k to 20
Remove regularization
Use a group-aware split such as `GroupKFold`, so no patient is in both training and validation
e:
Images of the same patient are very similar. With a random split, the model sees the same patient in training and in validation, so it can recognize the patient instead of the disease. That is leakage between rows.
Group splits keep all rows of a group (patient, user, device) on one side.
The validation should mimic real use: new patients, new hospitals.
r: Split by group when rows are not independent.

q: What happens when you increase the penalty strength `alpha` in ridge regression?
o: Coefficients grow, which lowers bias and raises variance
Coefficients shrink, which raises bias and lowers variance
Some coefficients become exactly zero
Only the intercept changes
e:
The penalty makes large coefficients expensive, so the model is pulled toward simpler fits. A simpler fit follows the training data less closely (more bias) but changes less between samples (less variance).
Too much penalty underfits; too little leaves overfitting. Choose `alpha` with cross-validation.
Ridge shrinks coefficients but does not zero them out; that is lasso (L1).
r: More regularization: more bias, less variance.

q: Which model is most affected if you forget to scale numeric features that have very different ranges?
o: Random forest
Gradient-boosted trees
Decision tree
k-nearest neighbours
e:
k-nearest neighbours compares distances. A feature measured in thousands (salary) swamps one measured in units (number of children), so scaling changes which points are neighbours.
Tree-based models split on thresholds one feature at a time, so a monotonic rescaling does not change their splits.
SVMs, linear models with regularization and neural networks also need scaling.
r: Distance and penalty methods need scaling; trees do not.

q: How does gradient boosting build its ensemble?
o: It adds small trees one at a time, each trained to correct the errors of the current ensemble
It trains one tree and prunes it by cross-validation
It trains deep trees independently on bootstrap samples and averages them
It picks the best of many random trees
e:
Boosting is sequential. Each new shallow tree fits the gradient of the loss (roughly, the errors left) of what has been built so far, and its contribution is scaled by a learning rate.
That mostly lowers bias, while a random forest mostly lowers variance.
Too many trees or too high a learning rate can overfit, so use early stopping on a validation set.
r: Boosting: sequential, each tree fixes the last errors.

q: A random forest ranks a customer ID column among its most important features when using the default impurity-based importance. What is a better check?
o: Trust the ranking: the forest saw the data
Drop the columns with the lowest importance and retrain
Permutation importance computed on held-out data
Add more trees until the ranking stabilizes
e:
Impurity-based importance is computed on the training data and favours features with many distinct values, like IDs, because they let trees split into tiny pure groups. That is memorization, not signal.
Permutation importance shuffles one feature at a time on held-out data and measures how much the score drops, so useless features get a value near zero.
It can still mislead when features are strongly correlated.
r: Prefer permutation importance on held-out data.

q: You pick the 20 features most correlated with the label on the full dataset, then run cross-validation on those 20. Why is the score too optimistic?
o: Twenty features are too few
The selection used the labels of the validation folds, so it leaks information; it must be done inside each training fold
Cross-validation cannot be used after feature selection
Correlation is not a valid way to rank features
e:
Choosing features with the labels of all rows lets the validation rows influence which features are kept. With many candidate features, some correlate with the label by chance, and the CV score then looks good.
Put feature selection inside the pipeline so it is fitted again on each training fold.
Correlation is a fair first filter; the mistake is where in the process it runs.
r: Selection is part of training: do it inside CV.

q: What does `class_weight="balanced"` do in scikit-learn classifiers such as `LogisticRegression`?
o: It duplicates rows of the minority class
It removes rows of the majority class
It weights each class inversely to its frequency, so mistakes on the rare class cost more
It sets the decision threshold to match the class ratio
e:
The data stays the same. Each sample gets a weight of n_samples / (n_classes × n_samples_of_its_class), so errors on rare examples count more in the loss.
This often gives results close to oversampling without copying rows.
It changes the model's probabilities, so recalibrate them if you need real probabilities.
r: Class weights make rare-class errors cost more.

q: A model says "fraud, 90% probability", but only 70% of such cases are really fraud. What is this problem called?
o: Class imbalance
Underfitting
Data leakage
Poor calibration: the probabilities do not match the observed frequencies
e:
A calibrated model is right about 70% of the time when it says 70%. A good ranking (high AUC) can come with overconfident probabilities, which matters when you use them in decisions such as expected costs.
Check it with a reliability (calibration) curve. Fix it with Platt scaling or isotonic regression, fitted on data the model did not train on.
r: A good ranking does not mean honest probabilities.

q: How would you choose evaluation metrics for a fraud detection model?
a:
- Start from the business: what does a missed fraud cost, and what does a false alarm cost (review time, annoyed customers)?
- Fraud is rare, so skip accuracy. Use precision, recall and PR-AUC; ROC-AUC is a secondary view.
- Fix an operating point: for example the best recall at a precision the review team can handle, or the threshold that minimises expected cost.
- Split by time, not at random, and keep the latest period as the test set.
- Check segments (new customers, countries, amounts) for hidden weak spots.
- After launch, track the same metrics on labelled cases, plus the number of alerts per day.

q: A shop's app starts attracting a younger audience and the model gets worse, although how age relates to buying has not changed. Which kind of drift is this?
o: Concept drift
Covariate shift: the input distribution changed
Data leakage
Label shift
e:
Covariate shift: the distribution of the inputs P(x) changes, while the relation P(y | x) stays the same. The model sees more of a region where it had little data and is less accurate there.
Concept drift is when P(y | x) itself changes, for example when customer behaviour changes after a price rise. Label shift is when the share of each class changes.
Covariate shift can often be detected without labels, by comparing input distributions.
r: Covariate shift: the inputs change. Concept drift: the rule changes.

q: The labels for your model's predictions arrive about 60 days later. How do you monitor the model in the meantime?
o: Track input data quality and the feature and prediction distributions against a reference as early warnings, and compute the real metrics when labels arrive
Monitor only latency and error rates of the service
Retrain every night and assume it fixes everything
You cannot: wait for the labels
e:
Without labels you cannot measure accuracy, but you can see symptoms: missing values, changed ranges, shifts in feature distributions or in the share of predicted positives.
These are alarms, not proof: a shift does not always hurt accuracy. When labels arrive, compute the real metrics (grouped by prediction date) and compare.
Latency and errors are needed too, but they say nothing about quality.
r: No labels yet: watch the inputs and the predictions.

q: A feature is computed with SQL for training but re-implemented in the serving code, and the online values differ slightly. What is this called and what is the best fix?
o: Training-serving skew; use one shared definition of the feature (or log the serving values and train on them)
Overfitting; add regularization
Concept drift; retrain more often
Data leakage; remove the feature
e:
Training-serving skew is a difference between the data the model was trained on and what it gets in production, here caused by two implementations of one feature.
The fixes: compute the feature with the same code (or a feature store) in both places, or log the exact values at serving time and train on those logs, and test that offline and online values match.
Retraining does not help if the two pipelines disagree.
r: Same feature code for training and serving.

q: A new ranking model improves the offline metric, but click-through falls in the online A/B test. What is the most plausible explanation?
o: The A/B testing tool must be buggy
The model needs more regularization
The offline data only reflects what the old system showed, and the offline metric is only a proxy for the goal, so the improvement did not carry over
The test set was too large
e:
Logged data only contains items the old system chose to show, so the model is evaluated on a biased sample (selection bias) and its choices outside that sample are never checked. The offline metric, such as NDCG on logged clicks, is also only a proxy for the goal.
The online experiment measures the real effect, so trust it, after checking the sample size and that users were assigned at random.
Use offline metrics to filter candidates and online tests to decide.
r: Offline metrics are proxies; the A/B test decides.

q: When and why do you use nested cross-validation?
a:
- Problem: if you choose hyperparameters with cross-validation and then report that same score, the number is optimistic, because the best result was picked.
- Outer loop: splits the data into k folds to estimate performance on unseen data.
- Inner loop: inside each outer training part, runs a separate cross-validation (for example a grid search) to choose the hyperparameters.
- Report the average of the outer test scores: it estimates the whole procedure "tune and fit", not one fixed model.
- It costs k times the search. Use it with small datasets or to compare model families fairly; with a lot of data a held-out test set is enough.
- The final model is then tuned on all the data with one more search.

q: A missed fraud costs 50 and a false alarm costs 1. If the model's probabilities are well calibrated, at which predicted probability of fraud should you start flagging payments?
o: About 0.02
About 0.98
e:
Flag when the expected cost of ignoring is higher than the cost of flagging: p × 50 > (1 - p) × 1, which gives p > 1 / 51, about 0.02.
The default of 0.5 is only right when both errors cost the same. 0.98 flips the costs.
This works only if the probabilities are calibrated, so check calibration first.
r: Threshold = cost of a false alarm / (cost of a false alarm + cost of a miss).

q: A model had a great cross-validation score but disappoints in production. What do you check?
a:
- Leakage: features only known after the outcome, preprocessing or feature selection fitted on all the data, duplicated rows, or the same entity in both training and validation.
- Split design: random splits on time-ordered or grouped data instead of splits by time or by group.
- Training-serving skew: different feature code, missing values, units or time zones online.
- Drift: has the input distribution, or the behaviour behind the labels, changed since the training period?
- Population: does production traffic include cases that never appeared in the training data (selection bias)?
- Metric: is the offline metric a good proxy for the product goal, and was the threshold set for production costs?
- Compare offline and online feature values for the same cases to find the first difference.

q: A lender trains a default model only on past loans that were approved, then uses it to score all applicants. What is the main risk?
o: Class imbalance
Concept drift
Underfitting because there are too few features
Selection bias: there are no outcomes for the kind of applicants who used to be rejected, so scores for them are unreliable
e:
Outcomes (repaid or defaulted) exist only for approved applicants, so the training sample is not representative of everyone who will be scored. The model extrapolates for groups the old policy excluded, and an evaluation on approved loans looks better than reality.
Mitigations: a small controlled group that is approved regardless, reject inference techniques (used with care), conservative thresholds at first, and monitoring of the new population.
Cross-validation cannot detect this, because every fold shares the same bias.
r: Labels exist only where past decisions allowed them.
